tagline: A river runs between the roadways of an early automobile parkway
intro: The Bronx River Parkway follows its namesake river through Westchester, with wooded stretches and roadways that separate with the river between them. Its 13.2-mile Westchester section, from the Bronx county line to Kensico Dam Plaza, is a New York State Scenic Byway. NYSDOT identifies scenic, historical and recreational qualities, including the road’s pioneering use of a median and bridges for crossing streets. North of White Plains, junctions are controlled by traffic lights.

Construction began in Westchester in 1907, making this the country’s earliest limited-access automobile route to begin construction. The Long Island Motor Parkway started a year later but opened a section in 1908, before the Bronx River road. After delays, the remaining Westchester construction began in 1917; sections opened in 1922 and 1925. Later rebuilding widened the stretch between Bronxville and the Bronx and replaced intersections with overpasses or separated interchanges.

Start southbound at Kensico Circle, within sight of the dam, and follow the river-and-rail corridor toward White Plains. Continue through Scarsdale to the wooded separation of the roadways in Yonkers. Below the Sprain Brook junction at Bronxville, the road takes on its controlled-access commuter character. The scenic designation ends at the Bronx line, although the parkway continues south.

moments.title: Kensico Dam
moments.text: Kensico Dam rises 307 feet above its foundation at the parkway’s northern end. The earlier dam, built in 1885, could not meet New York’s growing demand for water. Demolition began in 1911; construction of the replacement followed in 1913 and finished in 1917, three years ahead of schedule. Engineer Frank E. Winsor directed construction, with crews made up largely of Italian immigrants. The reservoir required the flooding of Kensico village, whose families moved to surrounding communities after their land was condemned and appraised. History placards now stand throughout the plaza at the foot of the dam.

moments.title: White Plains
moments.text: Near the Cross Westchester Expressway, the parkway’s two roadways spread almost 400 feet apart before coming together again at Old Tarrytown Road. At the County Center, Central Avenue meets the parkway at a junction controlled by traffic lights. Farther south, the road passes the developed western edge of downtown White Plains. White Plains became the county seat in 1758. Its postwar shopping district drew customers from beyond the city as nearby parkways and expressways were built. The Bronx River Parkway crosses both the river and the railroad tracks within the city.

moments.title: Yonkers
moments.text: In the wooded stretch north of Leewood Drive, the Bronx River flows between the parkway’s separated roadways. The roadways curve through woods before drawing back toward the railway corridor at Crestwood. Building the parkway changed the neighborhood as well as the river corridor. Right-of-way purchases took Crestwood lots and divided cross streets. The Bronx River also separates Crestwood, in Yonkers, from the village of Tuckahoe. The Harlem Line follows the river, with its Crestwood station named for the neighborhood across the water. The nearby Crestwood station appeared on the cover of The Saturday Evening Post in 1946, in Norman Rockwell’s painting Commuters.
